slides.purpose: Introduce the presentation scope and set up the architectural discussion.
slides.key_message: Migrations provide repeatable, tracked structural changes to relational data stores.
slides.headline: Database Migrations in Production
slides.subtitle: Managing evolving application schemas reliably over time
slides.speaker_notes: Welcome. Today we will explore how database migrations function as the backbone of reliable application evolution.

slides.purpose: Establish the foundational definition provided in db-guide.
slides.key_message: Migrations are explicit change records for database schemas.
slides.headline: A migration records schema changes
slides.speaker_notes: At its heart, a migration records schema changes so that software and data structures remain synchronized across environments.

slides.purpose: Explain why recording changes in version control provides organizational benefits.
slides.key_message: Schema history belongs under version control with application logic.
slides.headline: Version control ensures auditability and repeatability
slides.body: Tracking changes in plain text allows database DDL to live beside application source code, leveraging standard review workflows.
bullets: Track modifications in source control alongside application code
Enable automated continuous integration testing against target versions
Maintain identical structural history across dev, staging, and production
slides.speaker_notes: When schema updates are committed as code files, every pull request can be audited and tested automatically before merge.

slides.purpose: Demonstrate the concrete implementation of a database migration file.
slides.key_message: Migrations specify explicit forward and rollback operations.
slides.headline: DDL operations define forward and backward steps
slides.caption: Reversible changes allow quick recovery when deployments fail.
slides.speaker_notes: Each migration file typically encapsulates explicit up steps and reversible down steps to guarantee controlled application of DDL.

slides.purpose: Highlight the operational challenges that formal migration tools prevent.
slides.key_message: Unmanaged manual schema changes present severe operational risks.
slides.headline: Direct production alterations introduce critical hazards
bullets: Locks on heavy tables cause cascading application timeouts
Irreversible data conversions risk permanent corruption
Mismatched deployment sequences cause transient runtime errors
slides.speaker_notes: Ad-hoc alterations in live environments often trigger lock contention or downtime. Standardizing migrations prevents these surprises.

slides.purpose: Present the industry-standard multi-phase migration strategy.
slides.key_message: The expand-and-contract pattern avoids downtime by maintaining compatibility across releases.
slides.headline: Expand and contract decouples schema and code releases
slides.speaker_notes: To achieve zero downtime, we separate database transitions into additive, dual-read/write, and cleanup phases.

slides.purpose: Detail the concrete steps of an expand-and-contract rollout.
slides.key_message: A phased rollout sequence keeps live traffic flowing during table updates.
slides.headline: Multi-phase rollouts prevent deployment deadlocks
slides.body: Running migrations during active traffic requires careful coordination between deployment pipelines and active database transactions.
bullets: Add new nullable columns or tables without breaking older code versions
Deploy updated code that writes to both old and new schema structures
Backfill legacy records incrementally via background worker batches
Remove obsolete columns only after old application versions retire
slides.speaker_notes: By never altering existing columns destructively while active services use them, rollouts remain safe and transparent to users.

slides.purpose: Provide tactical best practices for database CI/CD pipelines.
slides.key_message: Automated linting and timeouts safeguard critical workloads.
slides.headline: Guardrails prevent accidental table-level locking
bullets: Enforce strict timeouts on DDL locks to prevent query backlog
Validate migration idempotency across staging data snapshots
Disallow destructive operations without explicit operator review
Automate schema drift detection against the production catalog
slides.speaker_notes: Setting short lock timeouts ensures that if an exclusive lock cannot be acquired immediately, production traffic is not stalled behind it.

slides.purpose: Address developer workflow and multi-contributor coordination.
slides.key_message: Standardizing local development and merge practices prevents migration conflicts.
slides.headline: Consistent team conventions streamline collaboration
bullets: Coordinate sequential numbering or timestamps to avoid merge conflicts
Isolate schema changes from large-scale domain logic pull requests
Seed consistent baseline states for local integration environments
slides.speaker_notes: When multiple feature branches add migrations concurrently, clear conventions ensure migrations apply cleanly without manual conflict resolution.

slides.purpose: Summarize the value of treating schema evolution as a first-class engineering discipline.
slides.key_message: Automated, incremental schema management is essential for continuous delivery.
slides.headline: Reliable migrations enable confident continuous deployment
slides.speaker_notes: With disciplined migrations in place, teams deploy software updates multiple times a day without fear of database corruption or downtime.

slides.purpose: Introduce the deck topic and set context for a new engineer.
slides.key_message: Migrations are how software systems evolve database structure reliably over time.
slides.headline: Understanding Database Migrations

slides.speaker_notes: Welcome to the team. Today we will cover what database migrations are and how we use them to evolve our systems safely.

slides.purpose: Anchor the presentation on the fundamental definition provided in the source documentation.
slides.key_message: A migration serves as an explicit record of schema modifications.
slides.headline: A migration records schema changes.
slides.speaker_notes: At its most fundamental level, a migration is simply a durable record of schema changes made to the database.

slides.purpose: Explain the underlying problem that migrations solve.
slides.key_message: Unrecorded manual schema updates lead to unmaintainable systems.
slides.headline: Manual changes create silent divergence
slides.body: Without structured migrations, shared environments drift out of sync, making manual updates error-prone and untracked.
bullets: Eliminates manual DDL commands in production
Prevents environment drift across stages
Provides reproducible database setups locally
slides.speaker_notes: Before migrations, developers ran scripts manually, causing dev, staging, and production databases to fall completely out of alignment.

slides.purpose: Illustrate how migrations interact with version control systems.
slides.key_message: Migrations live inside source control just like application code.
slides.headline: Schema evolution belongs in version control
bullets: Committed directly alongside application code
Reviewed through regular pull request workflows
Preserves an auditable timeline of every table update
Guarantees that state can be inspected at any historical commit
slides.speaker_notes: We treat database modifications like any other piece of code: tracked in git, reviewed in PRs, and deployed systematically.

slides.purpose: Show a concrete example of what a migration file looks like.
slides.key_message: Migrations encapsulate deterministic SQL DDL statements.
slides.headline: Changes are expressed as ordered files
slides.caption: A typical forward-moving schema modification file.
slides.speaker_notes: Here is a clean example of a migration file. It applies a specific schema addition predictably across all environments.

slides.purpose: Explain the bidirectional structure common to most migration frameworks.
slides.key_message: Well-designed migrations define forward and reverse operational steps.
slides.headline: Migrations define both apply and revert operations
slides.body: Most migration engines support both forward transitions and rollback operations, keeping changes reversible when appropriate.
bullets: Up transitions apply the new schema modifications
Down transitions safely revert the corresponding changes
Automated tools run unapplied files sequentially
slides.speaker_notes: When you write a migration, you generally think about two directions: applying the modification and unwinding it if things go wrong.

slides.purpose: Demystify how migration engines determine which files need execution.
slides.key_message: An internal history table prevents migrations from running more than once.
slides.headline: The database tracks its own historical log
bullets: A dedicated metadata table records executed migration files
The migration runner compares directory files against logged runs
Only newly committed files execute against the target database
Checksums verify that existing scripts have not been modified
slides.speaker_notes: How does a tool know what to run? It checks a tracking table inside the database itself that lists every executed migration.

slides.purpose: Introduce the golden rule of zero-downtime database changes in production.
slides.key_message: Zero-downtime updates require database changes that support both old and new application code.
slides.headline: Every migration must remain backwards-compatible.
slides.speaker_notes: During deployments, older application pods run alongside newer ones. Your migration must never break running instances of older code.

slides.purpose: Walk through the expand-and-contract operational pattern.
slides.key_message: Multi-phase rollouts prevent locks and data outages.
slides.headline: Execute complex schema shifts in stages
slides.body: To safely alter tables in high-traffic applications, split destructive operations across multiple deployment phases.
